description: Visual, verbal, manual and mechanical guidance and the four types of feedback used to improve performance.
content_html:
Guidance: How Coaches Communicate a Skill

Before a performer can improve, they need to understand what the skill looks like and how to produce it. Guidance is the process by which a coach communicates the nature of a skill to the learner. The four types of guidance — visual, verbal, manual and mechanical — differ in the channel through which the information is delivered, and each has specific advantages and disadvantages that make it more or less appropriate for different learners, skill types and stages of learning.

Visual Guidance

Visual guidance shows the performer what the correct movement looks like. A coach demonstrating a tennis backhand, a video of Adam Peaty’s breaststroke technique or a slow-motion replay of a gymnastic routine are all examples of visual guidance. Visual guidance is highly effective for beginners who do not yet have a clear mental image of the skill — seeing the movement creates a cognitive model for the performer to try to replicate. It is also effective for observational learners and for skills where timing and spatial awareness are critical.

However, visual guidance has limits. A demonstration by the coach or an elite performer may be too fast or too technically advanced for a beginner to process fully. If the demonstration is inaccurate, the learner will attempt to replicate the error. Video footage helps overcome the speed problem (slow motion replay) but requires technology that may not always be available. Cognitive overload can occur if too much visual information is presented at once — showing a beginner a full complex gymnastics routine before breaking it down can be counter-productive.

Verbal Guidance

Verbal guidance uses spoken language to describe or cue the skill. A coach saying “keep your elbow high on the follow-through” or “bend your knees as you receive the pass” is providing verbal guidance. Verbal guidance is quick, flexible and requires no equipment. It is especially valuable when a correction needs to be made mid-session, or when a specific part of a technique needs to be highlighted after a demonstration.

The main disadvantage of verbal guidance is that it relies entirely on the performer’s ability to translate spoken words into physical movement. For beginners, complex verbal instructions can overload working memory. The effectiveness of verbal guidance also depends on the coach’s clarity and the learner’s listening skills. Key phrases — cue words — are a refined form of verbal guidance that reduce cognitive load: “hips first,” “eyes on the target,” “tight core” distil a complex instruction into a single memorable trigger.

Manual Guidance

Manual guidance involves the coach physically guiding the performer through the correct movement. A gymnastics coach supporting a young child through a forward roll, a swimming teacher holding a beginner’s hips to help them feel horizontal body position, or a tennis coach physically moving a player’s arm through the correct backhand motion are all examples of manual guidance. Manual guidance is particularly useful for beginners learning dangerous movements (where the physical support prevents injury) and for helping a performer feel the kinaesthetic sensation of the correct technique.

The main disadvantage is that the performer may become dependent on the physical support and be unable to replicate the movement without it. There is also a safeguarding consideration — physical contact requires appropriate consent and must be handled carefully. Manual guidance is most effective when it is used to establish an initial feel for the movement and then progressively withdrawn as the performer begins to internalise the skill.

Key Fact

Four guidance types: Visual (see the skill; may overload beginners), Verbal (spoken cues; relies on translation to movement), Manual (physical contact; risk of dependency), Mechanical (apparatus support; removes fear but not natural movement). All four can be combined effectively and the appropriate choice depends on the learner’s stage, the skill’s demands and available resources.

Mechanical Guidance

Mechanical guidance uses equipment to physically support or constrain the learner’s movement. A swimming lane float that supports the legs, a trampoline harness that keeps a gymnast safe during aerial work or a batting tee that positions the ball for a beginner cricketer are all mechanical guidance. Like manual guidance, mechanical guidance helps the performer feel the correct movement and removes fear from dangerous or unfamiliar skills.

The disadvantage is that the supported movement is not always identical to the natural, unsupported movement. A swimmer who relies on a float is not using the same body position they will use in competition. Mechanical guidance is most effective as a stepping stone — it builds confidence and the initial motor pattern, but must be phased out as the performer progresses.

Feedback: Information After Performance

Feedback is information received about the quality of a performance. Without feedback, learning is slow or impossible — a performer who practises with errors repeatedly simply automates those errors. Edexcel identifies four types of feedback: intrinsic, extrinsic, concurrent and terminal.

Intrinsic feedback comes from the performer’s own sensory systems. A gymnast who feels that their landing was heavy and unbalanced, or a bowler who feels that the release of the ball was too early, is receiving intrinsic feedback. It is immediate and constant — available during every movement — but requires experience and developed kinaesthetic awareness to interpret accurately. Beginners often cannot distinguish between correct and incorrect “feel” because they have no established reference point.

Extrinsic feedback comes from an external source outside the performer. A coach calling “push through the hips” from the sideline, a video replay showing a fault in the golf swing, or the sound of the crowd’s reaction to a goal are all extrinsic feedback. Extrinsic feedback is particularly valuable for beginners who cannot yet accurately interpret their own intrinsic sensations, because the external source provides an objective reference point.

Concurrent and Terminal Feedback

Concurrent feedback is delivered during the execution of the skill. A coach walking alongside a swimmer calling “higher elbow, higher elbow” during a training length, or a dance teacher calling corrections as students move through a routine, is providing concurrent feedback. It is very immediate and can prevent errors from continuing, but it can also distract the performer or interfere with their focus during a complex skill.

Terminal feedback is delivered after the performance has finished. A coach who reviews video footage with an athlete after a training session, or who gives a critique at the end of a drill, is providing terminal feedback. It allows a more considered analysis and is less disruptive to the performance itself, but there is a delay between the movement and the information, which can make it harder for the performer to connect the feedback to what they did.

A very common error is to conflate these two dimensions of feedback. Intrinsic and extrinsic describe the SOURCE of feedback (from within the performer vs from outside). Concurrent and terminal describe the TIMING of feedback (during vs after performance). They are completely separate dimensions. Intrinsic feedback can only be concurrent (you feel something during a movement). Extrinsic feedback can be concurrent (coach shouts during a drill) or terminal (coach reviews with player after the match). Always explain which dimension you are using and avoid treating “intrinsic” as if it means the same as “concurrent.”

Beginners benefit most from visual guidance (demonstration), manual or mechanical guidance (physical support), extrinsic feedback (coach’s objective eye) and terminal feedback (considered review after practice). Advanced performers benefit more from verbal cue words (minimal interference), intrinsic feedback (tuning their own kinaesthetic sense) and concurrent feedback from a specialist coach. Matching the type to the learner’s stage is a core coaching principle — and a common focus of 6- and 9-mark exam questions in this unit.

Key Fact

Matching guidance and feedback to the learner’s stage: beginners need visual/manual guidance and extrinsic terminal feedback (objective reference they cannot generate themselves). Advanced performers rely more on verbal cues, intrinsic feedback and concurrent feedback from specialist coaches.
exam_tip_html: Edexcel’s primary feedback classification is Concurrent/Terminal (by TIMING) and Intrinsic/Extrinsic (by SOURCE) — not Knowledge of Results/Knowledge of Performance, which is a different taxonomy. Always name the type, define it in one sentence, and apply it to the sporting context in the question. A common error is to describe “positive” and “negative” feedback without explaining what they mean: positive feedback confirms what was correct (reinforcing the movement); negative feedback identifies what was wrong (corrective). For 4-mark Discuss questions about guidance, explore both an advantage AND a disadvantage of the type named in the question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Four guidance types: Visual (seeing the skill), Verbal (spoken cues), Manual (physical contact) and Mechanical (apparatus support). Each has advantages and disadvantages; selection depends on the learner’s stage, skill complexity and available resources.
  • Four feedback types by source and timing: Intrinsic (from within, during movement), Extrinsic (from outside, from coach/video), Concurrent (during performance) and Terminal (after performance). These are separate dimensions that can combine.
  • Beginners benefit from extrinsic, visual guidance and terminal feedback; advanced performers can use intrinsic, verbal and concurrent feedback effectively. Matching guidance/feedback type to learner stage is a key coaching principle.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following describes manual guidance?
A) A coach explaining the technique verbally
B) A performer watching a video of themselves
C) A coach physically moving the performer through the movement
D) Using a harness to support aerial work
practice_questions.marks: C) A coach physically moving the performer through the movement [1 mark]. Option D describes mechanical guidance (apparatus); option A is verbal; option B is visual.

practice_questions.text: Define 'concurrent feedback' and give one sporting example.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for correctly defining concurrent feedback: information given during the performance of a skill as the movement is happening. 1 mark for a valid sporting example (e.g. a swimming coach calling corrections from the poolside as the swimmer completes a training length / a dance teacher calling adjustments while students perform a routine).

practice_questions.text: Explain one advantage and one disadvantage of visual guidance when teaching a beginner a new sport skill.
practice_questions.marks: Up to 3 marks: 1 mark for stating an advantage of visual guidance (e.g. it gives the beginner a clear cognitive model of what the correct movement looks like, which is essential when they have no prior experience of the skill); 1 mark for stating a disadvantage (e.g. an expert-level demonstration may be too fast or technically advanced for a beginner to process, leading to cognitive overload); 1 mark for applying both points to a specific sporting scenario (e.g. showing a beginner a full-speed gymnastics vault demonstration may confuse rather than guide them, whereas a slower, broken-down demo would be more effective).

practice_questions.text: A club badminton coach is working with a 14-year-old beginner learning the overhead clear. Discuss whether verbal or visual guidance is more appropriate at this stage of learning.
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for defining or describing each guidance type in the context (verbal: spoken instruction such as 'hit high and deep'; visual: demonstration of the stroke by the coach or video). 1 mark for arguing in favour of visual guidance for this beginner (the learner does not yet have a cognitive model of the overhead clear; a demonstration provides a complete picture of the movement; beginners benefit from seeing before being told). 1 mark for arguing limitations of verbal guidance for this learner (a beginner may not yet have the kinaesthetic vocabulary to translate complex verbal instructions into physical movement). 1 mark for a justified conclusion (visual guidance is likely more appropriate initially because it provides the mental model the beginner needs before verbal cues can be meaningful; verbal guidance can be added as a refinement tool once the basic pattern is established).

practice_questions.text: A county-level netball coach provides feedback to players during and after matches. Analyse the relative value of concurrent and terminal feedback for improving player performance.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Both feedback types clearly defined; advantages and disadvantages of each discussed with accurate physiological or psychological reasoning; consistent application to netball; comparative analysis; conclusion reached.

Secure: Both types defined; advantages of each present; mostly applied to netball; some comparison; conclusion present.

Developing: One feedback type more fully analysed; limited comparison; some sporting application.

Emerging: Basic description of the two types with little analysis or application.

Acceptable content: concurrent advantages — immediate correction prevents errors from being repeated within the same session; particularly useful for technical cues during lower-intensity drills; concurrent disadvantages — can distract a player during a high-pressure match situation; complex concurrent instructions may overload working memory during fast-paced play; terminal advantages — allows considered, detailed review after match footage; performer is not distracted during play; can be supported by video; terminal disadvantages — delay between movement and information makes it harder to connect the feedback to the specific action; player memory of the relevant moment may have faded. Conclusion: both types have a role; concurrent feedback is valuable during training drills; terminal feedback is best for post-match analysis of patterns and tactical decisions.

practice_questions.text: A gymnastics coach works with performers at different stages of learning. Evaluate which guidance and feedback strategies are most effective for beginners compared to advanced performers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Full evaluation contrasting beginners (visual, manual, mechanical guidance; extrinsic, terminal feedback) with advanced performers (verbal cue words, minimal mechanical support; intrinsic, concurrent feedback); mechanisms explained (beginners lack kinaesthetic awareness; advanced performers can interpret their own sensations); consistent gymnastics application throughout; balanced, justified conclusion.

Secure: Both learner stages addressed; at least two guidance and two feedback types compared; generally accurate; some gymnastics application; conclusion present.

Developing: One stage more fully developed; limited feedback comparison; some sporting application.

Emerging: Basic description of guidance or feedback with little comparison of learner stages.

Beginners: visual (demonstration of vault or routine gives a cognitive model); manual (coach physically supporting learner through a forward roll prevents injury and establishes feel); mechanical (harness in aerial work removes fear); extrinsic (coach provides objective information the beginner cannot generate internally); terminal (post-drill review is less disruptive than concurrent instructions during a fragile beginner movement).

Advanced: verbal cue words (minimal distraction, triggers trained movement patterns); rely more on intrinsic feedback (tuned kinaesthetic sense from years of practice); concurrent feedback from a specialist coach may be valuable for subtle corrections; less reliance on mechanical support which would alter the movement dynamics. Conclusion: guidance and feedback selection must be matched to the learner’s stage; what helps a beginner internalise a new skill can actually hinder an advanced performer who has already automated their technique.

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of feedback comes from the performer's own sensory systems during movement?
Which type of guidance uses apparatus or equipment to support the performer through the correct movement?
Feedback given AFTER the performance has finished is called _____ feedback.
A coach physically moving a gymnast through the correct movement is providing _____ guidance.
Match each feedback type to its description:
right: Delivered during the skill, as movement happens
Comes from within the performer's own sensory systems
Comes from an external source such as a coach

flashcard_questions.a: Guidance delivered through demonstration, video or modelling by an expert.
A coach physically moves the performer through the correct movement pattern.
Apparatus or equipment that supports the performer and constrains movement into the correct pattern.
Information from the performer's own sensory systems generated during movement.
Information from an external source such as a coach, video or scoreboard.
Feedback delivered during the performance of the skill as it is happening.
Feedback given after the performance has ended.

flashcard_questions.q: Why might manual guidance cause dependency?
flashcard_questions.a: The performer may be unable to replicate the movement without the physical support.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is visual guidance most effective for beginners?
flashcard_questions.a: It provides a cognitive model of the correct movement before they attempt it.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is verbal guidance less effective for beginners than advanced performers?
flashcard_questions.a: Beginners struggle to translate complex spoken instructions into physical movement.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the key difference between concurrent and terminal feedback?
flashcard_questions.a: Concurrent is given during the skill; terminal is given after the performance ends.

flashcard_questions.q: Why is intrinsic feedback less reliable for beginners?
flashcard_questions.a: Beginners have not yet developed the kinaesthetic awareness to interpret their own sensations accurately.

glossary_terms.definition: Information or instruction given before or during skill execution to help the performer understand the correct movement pattern.
Guidance delivered through what the performer sees, such as demonstrations, video footage or modelling by an expert.
Guidance delivered through spoken words, including instructions, explanations and cue words used by a coach.
Guidance delivered through physical contact, where the coach physically moves the learner through the correct movement pattern.
Guidance that uses apparatus or equipment to support the performer and constrain or direct the movement into the correct pattern.
Information received about a performance that allows the performer to evaluate their execution and guide future attempts.
Feedback that comes from within the performer, generated by their own sensory systems during movement.
Feedback that comes from an external source outside the performer, such as a coach, video replay or spectator response.
Feedback given during the performance of the skill, as the movement is happening.
Feedback given after the performance has ended, allowing the performer to reflect on their execution.
